28:4.text: And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you?

provenance.route: Mark 10:35-40, with the wording of Matthew 20:32 and Mark 10:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The King James Bible puts this question three times and never elsewhere. “what will ye that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:32; “that I should do unto” occurs in exactly one, Mark 10:51. 3 Nephi 28:4 reads ‘What will ye that I should do unto you’ — the opening of Matthew 20:32 welded to the closing of Mark 10:51. Mark 10:36, ‘What would ye that I should do for you?’, is the same question asked not of blind beggars but of two disciples, and it is prompted at Mark 10:35 by ‘we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire’ — the verb 3 Nephi 28:1 uses twice, ‘What is it that ye desire of me’.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the whole chapter is Mark 10:35-40 answered the other way. There the two who ask are James and John, the request is for places in the kingdom, and the reply is a refusal: ye know not what ye ask, and to sit on my right hand and on my left is not mine to give. Here twelve are asked what they desire, nine ask for a place in the kingdom and get it (28:3, ‘with me ye shall find rest’), and three ask for something else and are told they are more blessed. Two verses later the disciple whose desire is named as the precedent is John — one of the two who asked in Mark 10:35. The Book of Mormon is not quoting the Zebedee request; it is granting it.

28:4.note: ‘And when he had spake unto them, he turned himself unto the three, and said unto them, What will ye that I should do unto you, when I am gone unto the Father?’ Eight words that exist in the KJV only as two halves of two Synoptic questions, put in the setting of the third. The frame is set at 28:1, where the question is asked of all twelve with ‘desire’, Mark 10:35’s word; 1830 reads ‘when he had spake’, regularised to ‘spoken’ in 1920. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as an allusion, not a quotation.

28:6.text: Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.

provenance.other: “the disciple whom Jesus loved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 21:20, and “if I will that he tarry till I come” occurs in exactly two, John 21:22 and 21:23, which are one sentence reported twice. 3 Nephi 28:6 has ‘John, my beloved, which was with me in my ministry’. The dating clause is traceable too: “lifted up the Son of man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:28, where Jesus says it to the Jews — which is exactly what ‘before that I was lifted up by the Jews’ makes of it. 1830’s relative ‘which’ is modernised to ‘who’ in 1920 at both points in this verse.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is in the half of John 21 the Book of Mormon does not quote. John 21:23 exists to correct a rumour: ‘Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die; but, If I will that he tarry till I come.’ The evangelist is denying the very thing 3 Nephi 28 asserts. So the source text of the three Nephites is the New Testament’s own retraction of the belief that a disciple would not die — and this chapter takes the retracted reading, makes it explicit doctrine (28:7, ‘ye shall never taste of death’), and extends it to three more men. Reading the two together, the Book of Mormon does not merely echo John 21; it overrules its footnote.

28:6.note: ‘Behold, I know your thoughts, and ye have desired the thing which John, my beloved, which was with me in my ministry, before that I was lifted up by the Jews, desired of me.’ The verse names John, calls him beloved in the epithet the KJV uses of him in one verse only, and refers to a request of his which the Bible reports only at John 21:21-22. Hardy cross-references John 21:20-24 here.

28:6.text: Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me.

provenance.route: Job 21:27 for the wording, the Synoptic thought-reading formula for the situation → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “I know your thoughts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 21:27, and the four words run on identically: ‘Behold, I know your thoughts’. The Gospels have Jesus reading thoughts repeatedly — Matthew 9:4 ‘Jesus knowing their thoughts’, Luke 6:8 ‘he knew their thoughts’, Luke 11:17 ‘he, knowing their thoughts’ — but always as third-person narration and never in his own mouth. The KJV’s only first-person form belongs to Job.
provenance.significance: The split is the finding: the situation is the Gospels’ and the sentence is Job’s. What the Synoptics report about Jesus from outside, 3 Nephi 28:6 has him say about himself, and the only English the King James Bible offers for saying it is a line of Job’s accusing his comforters. Job’s next clause is ‘and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me’; here the thoughts known are a desire too holy to speak aloud (28:5, ‘they durst not speak unto him the thing which they desired’). The borrowed clause is turned from indictment to reassurance by the words that follow it.

28:6.note: Four consecutive words from the one KJV verse that has them, and the eye-catching ‘Behold’ with them. Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a): the verbal match is absolute and the contextual match is nil, which is the shape of a genuine borrowing of an idiom rather than of a passage.
28:6.whyNot: Job 21:27 is an accusation and 3 Nephi 28:6 is a disclosure of grace; nothing else of Job 21 is present, and ‘I know your thoughts’ is short enough and ordinary enough in its parts that a writer steeped in the KJV could produce it without reaching for Job. The Synoptic thought-reading scenes account for the idea; only the grammatical person requires Job.

28:7.text: Then said the Jews unto him, Now we know that thou hast a devil. Abraham is dead, and the prophets; and thou sayest, If a man keep my saying, he shall never taste of death.

provenance.route: John 8:52 for the phrase, Matthew 16:28 / Mark 9:1 / Luke 9:27 for the promise, Luke 21:26-27 for the coming → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “taste of death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 16:28, Mark 9:1, Luke 9:27 and John 8:52 — and the three Synoptic ones all read ‘shall not taste of death, till’. “never taste of death” occurs in exactly one, John 8:52. 3 Nephi 28:7 has John’s absolute adverb on the Synoptics’ promise. The rest of the sentence keeps counting: “coming in his kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 16:28; “come with power” occurs in exactly one, Mark 9:1; and “the powers of heaven” occurs in exactly one, Luke 21:26, whose next verse has the Son of man ‘coming in a cloud with power and great glory’ against this verse’s ‘when I shall come in my glory, with the powers of heaven’.
provenance.significance: Two suppressed contexts are doing the work. The first is John 8:52, where ‘he shall never taste of death’ is not a promise at all: it is the Jews quoting Jesus back at him as proof that he has a devil, since Abraham is dead and the prophets are dead. The Book of Mormon takes the sceptics’ formulation of the claim and grants it as fact. The second is the Synoptic saying itself, which is the New Testament’s own unfinished business — some standing here shall not taste of death till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom — a promise whose non-fulfilment John 21:23 is already managing. 3 Nephi 28 closes both loops at once by producing three men for whom the saying is literally true, and it does so in the exact words of all four verses.

28:7.note: ‘Therefore more blessed are ye, for ye shall never taste of death, but ye shall live to behold all the doings of the Father, unto the children of men, even until all things shall be fulfilled, according to the will of the Father, when I shall come in my glory, with the powers of heaven.’ Four KJV singletons converge in one sentence, one from each of the four verses that could supply it. This is the chapter’s densest verse and the one that shows the composition method plainly: the wording is John’s, the promise is Matthew’s and Mark’s, and the parousia clause is Luke’s.

28:8.text: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

provenance.other: “twinkling of an eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “we shall be changed” occurs in exactly one, both 1 Corinthians 15:52. The second clause is from the next verse: ‘this mortal must put on immortality’ (15:53) behind ‘from mortality to immortality’. “mortality” itself occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 5:4, so the abstract noun is not Paul’s word here; the Book of Mormon has abstracted it from his adjective, and Mormon 6:21 keeps the adjectival form ‘your mortal must put on immortality’.
provenance.significance: Paul’s sentence is strictly about the last trump: the dead raised incorruptible and the living changed, all at once, at the end. 3 Nephi 28:8 lifts the formula out of the eschaton and applies it to three men in the middle of history, and the text knows it has done so — 28:39 stops to say that ‘this change was not equal to that which should take place at the last day’. So the borrowing carries a qualification the source cannot supply, and 28:37-40 exists to supply it. The chapter borrows the resurrection’s vocabulary for something it then has to argue is not the resurrection.

28:8.note: ‘And ye shall never endure the pains of death; but when I shall come in my glory, ye shall be changed in the twinkling of an eye, from mortality to immortality.’ A KJV singleton reproduced word for word, with the verb 1 Corinthians 15:52 attaches to it, and the following verse’s antithesis behind the next clause. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold, but there is no question of the source.

28:9.text: Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.

provenance.other: “while the world standeth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 8:13. 3 Nephi 28:9 reads ‘while the world shall stand’ — the same idiom with the auxiliary future for the KJV’s present. No other English in the King James Bible measures a personal undertaking by the duration of the world.
provenance.significance: Paul’s one use of the phrase is a vow of permanent renunciation undertaken for somebody else’s sake: ‘I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.’ It is the strongest self-denial in the Pauline letters and its object is one weak brother’s conscience. 3 Nephi 28:9 sets the same measure on the same kind of vow at the largest possible scale — not meat but death forgone, not one brother but ‘the souls of men’ — and the sentence in which it does so is also about pain accepted for others (‘neither sorrow, save it be for the sins of the world’). Recover Paul’s context and the three Nephites’ request is a Corinthian scruple written large.

28:9.note: ‘And all this will I do because of the thing which ye have desired of me: for ye have desired that ye might bring the souls of men unto me, while the world shall stand.’ A KJV singleton with one auxiliary changed, in a clause whose logic — an indefinite personal cost accepted for the sake of others’ souls — is the logic of the verse it comes from.
28:9.whyNot: Four common words, and ‘while the world shall stand’ is natural English that a writer could reach independently; nothing else of 1 Corinthians 8 is in the chapter. The case is the absolute rarity plus the coincidence of situation, and a reasonable reader could decline it.

28:10.text: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.

provenance.route: Psalm 16:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Luke 13:29 and the Johannine ‘joy full’ formula in the same sentence
provenance.other: “fulness of joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 16:11, and 3 Nephi 28:10 has it twice. “sit down in the kingdom” occurs in exactly one, Luke 13:29 (Matthew 8:11 has ‘shall sit down with Abraham… in the kingdom of heaven’), against this verse’s ‘ye shall sit down in the kingdom of my Father’. “joy might be full” occurs in exactly one, John 15:11, and John 16:24 has ‘that your joy may be full’ against ‘your joy shall be full’ here. The closing chain — ‘ye shall be even as I am; and I am even as the Father; and the Father and I are one’ — is the John 17:21-22 unity language this catalogue adjudicates at 3 Nephi 19:23 and 19:29, and the phrase enters 3 Nephi at 27:31.
provenance.significance: Psalm 16:11 is a resurrection psalm in the New Testament’s own reading of it, and its ‘fulness of joy’ is located ‘in thy presence’ — a joy that consists in being where God is. 3 Nephi 28:10 keeps the location and makes it reciprocal: the Father has given Christ fulness of joy, Christ gives it to the three, and the giving ends in the unity formula of John 17. The Psalm supplies the noun, the Fourth Gospel supplies the mechanism by which it is transmitted, and Luke supplies the furniture of the kingdom the recipients sit down in.

28:10.note: ‘And for this cause ye shall have fulness of joy; and ye shall sit down in the kingdom of my Father; yea, your joy shall be full, even as the Father hath given me fulness of joy.’ Three KJV singletons in one sentence, from a Psalm, from Luke and from John. The mediation is genuinely undecided and is recorded as such: Psalm 16:11 is quoted at Acts 2:28, and tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence here because the Book of Mormon verse contains both the Psalm’s noun phrase (‘fulness of joy’) and a ‘joy… full’ clause close to Acts’ ‘full of joy’ — though that clause is better explained by John 15:11 and 16:24, which the verse also touches.

28:13.text: I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.

provenance.other: “caught up” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — 2 Corinthians 12:2, 12:4, 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and Revelation 12:5 — and only Paul’s two are ascents of a living man to heaven. “unspeakable words” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 12:4, and 28:13’s ‘unspeakable things’ is one noun away from it; 28:14’s ‘it was forbidden them that they should utter’ is 12:4’s ‘which it is not lawful for a man to utter’. “the heavens were opened” occurs in exactly two, Ezekiel 1:1 and Matthew 3:16 (Acts 7:56 reads ‘I see the heavens opened’).
provenance.significance: Paul’s rapture is unique in the New Testament and defiantly singular in its telling: one man, fourteen years ago, who cannot be named and cannot say whether he had a body. 3 Nephi 28:13-15 makes it corporate and datable — three men, named as a group, on the day Jesus departed — and keeps every element that made Paul’s account reticent. The prohibition is the tell. At 3 Nephi 19:34 this catalogue records the same verse of 2 Corinthians converted from prohibition to incapacity (the words ‘cannot be uttered by man’); here, fewer than ten chapters later, the prohibition is restored in Paul’s own terms — forbidden, not impossible. The book uses 2 Corinthians 12:4 twice and takes a different half of it each time.

28:13.note: ‘And behold, the heavens were opened, and they were caught up into heaven, and saw and heard unspeakable things.’ Three of Paul’s four distinctive elements in eighteen words, with the fourth (the uncertainty about the body) following at 28:15 as an eight-word run. Hardy cross-references 2 Corinthians 12:2-4 here. 1830 and 1920 agree.

28:15.text: And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;)

provenance.other: Eight consecutive words: ‘whether they were in the body or out of the body’ against ‘whether in the body, or out of the body’. “out of the body” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Job 20:25 (a sword drawn out of a body) and 2 Corinthians 12:2 and 12:3. The KJV’s verb for the other half of this verse is not present: “transfigured” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:2 and Mark 9:2, both of Jesus on the mountain, and the noun ‘transfiguration’ does not occur in the King James Bible at all.
provenance.significance: Two changes, and both are arguments. Paul writes ‘I cannot tell: God knoweth’ — a first-person confession of ignorance about his own state, offered as a reason for not boasting. 3 Nephi 28:15 makes it ‘they could not tell’, a narrator’s report about somebody else, and 28:17 then repeats the ignorance in Mormon’s own voice (‘whether they were mortal or immortal… I know not’) before 28:37 removes it by inquiry. Paul’s unresolvable question becomes a question the record answers. The second change is the noun: the chapter calls the event ‘a transfiguration’, a word the KJV never uses, formed from a verb the KJV uses of Christ alone. Paul’s rapture and the Synoptic mountain are fused, and the three disciples undergo in their own persons what in the King James Bible happens only to Jesus.

28:15.note: ‘And whether they were in the body or out of the body, they could not tell: for it did seem unto them like a transfiguration of them, that they were changed from this body of flesh, into an immortal state.’ An eight-word run from 2 Corinthians 12:3 with the pronoun turned from first person to third, and the strongest single verbal contact in the chapter. The 1830 and 1920 texts agree here.

28:16.text: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.

provenance.other: “heard and seen” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Luke 2:20, Philippians 4:9 and Revelation 22:8 — and only Luke’s has the full clause ‘the things that they had heard and seen’, against this verse’s ‘the things which they had heard and seen’, a one-word difference over seven. Acts 4:20 reverses the pair (‘the things which we have seen and heard’).
provenance.significance: Luke 2:20 is the KJV’s one sentence about witnesses going home to publish what they heard and saw — the shepherds returning, glorifying and praising God. 3 Nephi 28:16 is that sentence negated: they did again minister, but not of the things which they had heard and seen. The nearer situation is Acts 4:20, where apostles under an official prohibition answer ‘we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard’; the three Nephites are under a prohibition too, and they keep it. So the chapter takes the wording of the Bible’s most exuberant witnesses and the position of its most defiant ones, and produces silence.

28:16.note: ‘Nevertheless they did not minister of the things which they had heard and seen, because of the commandment which was given them in heaven.’ A seven-word near-run on a pairing the KJV has three times, in the negative.
28:16.whyNot: ‘Heard and seen’ is ordinary English and the only distinctive thing about the match is the order and the relative clause around it. Luke 2:20 has nothing else in common with this verse, and the situation — witnesses forbidden to speak — belongs to Acts 4, whose word order differs. Neither candidate is decisive on its own.

28:19.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

provenance.route: Acts 16:23-26, with Matthew 27:51’s phrase → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “rent in twain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the veil of the temple at the moment of the crucifixion. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase of a building at Alma 14:27, where the prison walls fall on the persecutors, and of the rocks at 3 Nephi 8:18. Acts 16:26 supplies the structure — preachers imprisoned by those outside the church, a violent opening of the prison, and the prisoners unhurt.
provenance.significance: This is the Alma 14 miracle re-run in a new book, and the row is written again for that reason (ADJUDICATING §4: across a book boundary, write the link). What is new here is the local resonance. Within 3 Nephi the phrase ‘rent in twain’ has already been used once, at 8:18, for the rocks that split at Christ’s death — the New World’s version of Matthew 27:51. When 28:19 uses it again for a prison that cannot hold his disciples, the same verb has run from the death of Christ to their deliverance, which is the movement Acts 16 makes in a single night and the Gospels make in three days.

28:19.note: ‘And they were cast into prison by them who did not belong to the church. And the prisons could not hold them, for they were rent in twain.’ The phrase is Matthew 27:51’s and the episode is Acts 16’s. The full argument for the phrase is made at Alma 14:27, where prison walls are rent in twain over the men who built them; this row records the borrowing re-entering in Mormon’s hand rather than restating it.

28:20.text: Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.

provenance.other: “depths of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 71:20, whose clause is ‘shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth’ against this verse’s ‘by his power they were delivered out of the depths of the earth’. 1830 reads ‘they could not dig pits sufficiently to hold them’, regularised to ‘sufficient’ in 1920.
provenance.significance: Psalm 71 is the prayer of a servant growing old: ‘Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation’ (71:18), and then the promise of being quickened again and brought up from the depths of the earth. That is precisely the condition the other nine disciples accepted at 28:2-3 — to live unto the age of man and then be taken — and precisely the condition these three declined. So the one KJV verse about being raised out of the earth belongs to a psalm about ageing into a ministry that outlasts a generation, which is the thing this chapter has just made permanent.

28:20.note: ‘And they were cast down into the earth. But they did smite the earth with the word of God, insomuch that by his power they were delivered out of the depths of the earth.’ A KJV singleton, in the one biblical sentence about being brought up again from where these men are buried.
28:20.whyNot: Four words, and the deliverance is a different kind: the psalmist is speaking figuratively of revival from trouble and near-death, the Book of Mormon literally of men dug out of pits. Nothing else of Psalm 71 is present.

28:21.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.route: Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 as paired by Hebrews 11:33-34 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Hebrews 11:33-34 sets the two deliverances side by side in adjacent clauses: “stopped the mouths of lions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:33, and “quenched the violence of fire” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 11:34. 3 Nephi 28:21-22 gives the same two in reverse order, furnace then beasts. There is no shared wording with either Daniel or Hebrews: “no harm” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses and none is Daniel’s (Daniel 3:27 has ‘the fire had no power’, Daniel 6:22 ‘they have not hurt me’). tools/mediation-check.py on Daniel 6:22 against Hebrews 11:33 returns no decisive divergence, because the Book of Mormon reproduces neither; the mediation is argued below rather than measured.
provenance.significance: The evidence that this is Hebrews’ catalogue and not Daniel’s stories is inside the Book of Mormon. Ether 12 is the book’s own chapter of faith-exemplars — its Hebrews 11 — and it names these same three men in Hebrews’ vocabulary: ‘it was by faith that the three disciples obtained a promise that they should not taste of death’ (Ether 12:17), where “obtained promises” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:33, the same verse that stops the mouths of lions. So the corpus reads the three Nephites through Hebrews 11 explicitly, and 3 Nephi 28:21-22 is what Hebrews 11:33-34 looks like when its list is turned back into narrative: the two Danielic deliverances, adjacent, unglossed, and multiplied (thrice, twice) because a catalogue of what faith does has no fixed number.

28:21.note: ‘And thrice they were cast into a furnace, and received no harm.’ With 28:22 this is Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 in two sentences, and the pairing — fire and beasts, in immediate succession, as instances of what happens to men under a promise — exists in the Bible in exactly one place, Hebrews 11:33-34. Catalogued as figural because there is no verbal contact at all; the case is the pairing plus Ether 12:17.
28:21.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared with Daniel or with Hebrews. Fire and wild beasts are the two standard ancient executions and any writer wanting invulnerable men could reach for both without a source, and the order is reversed from Hebrews’. The link rests entirely on the adjacency of the pair and on the Book of Mormon’s own use of Hebrews 11:33 at Ether 12:17.

28:22.text: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den.

provenance.other: “the sucking child shall play” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:8; “sucking child” occurs in exactly four and “shall play” in exactly two, of which Isaiah 11:8 is the only overlap. Isaiah 11:8 supplies the child, the playing and a den (‘the cockatrice’ den’); Isaiah 11:6 supplies the lamb and the little child among wild animals. 3 Nephi 28:22 has all four — a den, beasts, a child and a suckling lamb — in one clause. The Book of Mormon’s ‘suckling’ is not the KJV’s spelling, which is ‘sucking’ throughout, and 1830 and 1920 agree on it.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:6-8 is the peaceable kingdom: the wolf with the lamb, a little child leading them, the sucking child playing at the asp’s hole and the weaned child’s hand on the cockatrice’ den. It is the Book of Mormon’s standing image of the millennial future — the chapter is quoted whole at 2 Nephi 21 and its gathering verse is used as prophecy six chapters earlier at 3 Nephi 21:26. Here it is not prophesied but narrated: three men in a den of wild beasts, playing with them as a child plays with a lamb. The oracle is used as a description of what has already happened to somebody, which is what the chapter does to every eschatological text it touches — 1 Corinthians 15:52 at 28:8, Matthew 16:28 at 28:7.

28:22.note: ‘And twice were they cast into a den of wild beasts; and behold they did play with the beasts, as a child with a suckling lamb, and received no harm.’ Four of Isaiah 11:6-8’s images compressed into a single simile, including the KJV’s one instance of a child at play among dangerous animals.
28:22.whyNot: Only ‘play’ and ‘child’ survive in the KJV’s own form; ‘suckling’ is not the King James spelling, the lamb comes from a different verse than the den, and Isaiah’s den belongs to a cockatrice rather than to beasts. A writer describing a man unharmed among animals could reach for a child and a lamb with no Isaiah in view, which is why this is catalogued as an allusion at moderate confidence and marked uncertain for KJV-specificity.

28:29.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: “nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6, and “kindred, and tongue” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 5:9 and 14:6. The KJV’s four nouns at Revelation 14:6 are all singular: ‘to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people’. The 1830 text of 3 Nephi 28:29 reads ‘unto all nations, kindred, tongues and people’ — plural, singular, plural, plural — keeping the KJV’s singular ‘kindred’ stranded between two plurals; the 1920 edition regularised it to ‘kindreds’ and in doing so moved the phrase further from its source. The formula is used across the Book of Mormon and is adjudicated first at 1 Nephi 5:18.
provenance.significance: Worth a row for the orthographic datum rather than for the formula, which by 3 Nephi is the narrator’s own (CONVENTIONS §8). Revelation 14:6’s angel flies with the everlasting gospel to preach to every nation and kindred and tongue and people; 3 Nephi 28:29-30 has three men who ‘are as the angels of God’ doing exactly that among the scattered tribes. The apocalyptic figure and the ministry described are the same figure, and the verse that names it is the verse the Book of Mormon has been quoting for the phrase since 1 Nephi.

28:29.note: ‘They shall minister unto all the scattered tribes of Israel, and unto all nations, kindred, tongues and people.’ The Revelation 14:6 formula, whose argument is made at 1 Nephi 5:18; recorded here because the 1830 reading preserves the KJV’s singular ‘kindred’ and the modern text does not, and because the angel of Revelation 14:6 is what the next verse calls these men.

28:30.text: For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.

provenance.route: Matthew 22:30, with Luke 20:36’s argument → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “as the angels of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:30, and “in the resurrection they neither marry” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Mark 12:25 has ‘as the angels which are in heaven’ and Luke 20:36 ‘equal unto the angels’, so Matthew’s is the only form the Book of Mormon could be reproducing. 1830 reads ‘they can shew themselves unto whatsoever man it seemeth them good’, keeping the KJV’s ‘shew’; 1920 modernises it to ‘show’.
provenance.significance: Matthew’s sentence is about the resurrected, and the respect in which they are like angels is that they neither marry nor are given in marriage — which has nothing to do with the three Nephites. Luke’s parallel supplies the respect that does: ‘Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels’ (Luke 20:36). So 28:30 takes Matthew’s words and Luke’s reason. The chapter has done this twice already, at 28:7 (John’s adverb on Matthew’s promise) and 28:34 (Matthew’s verb in Luke’s polarity); it is the composition habit of the whole chapter, and it means the borrowings are being selected clause by clause rather than passage by passage.

28:30.note: ‘And they are as the angels of God, and if they shall pray unto the Father in the name of Jesus they can shew themselves unto whatsoever man it seemeth them good.’ Five words from the one KJV verse that has them, applied to men who have not died, on the strength of a clause found only in the Lukan parallel.

28:31.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, but “stand before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one: Romans 14:10, ‘we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ’. 2 Corinthians 5:10 has ‘appear before’. 3 Nephi 28:31 reads ‘when all people must surely stand before the judgement seat of Christ’ — Romans’ verb and Romans’ universal quantifier. 1830 spells ‘judgement’ and ‘marvellous’, both modernised in 1920.
provenance.significance: Paul’s clause is levelling. Its whole function at Romans 14:10 is to stop Christians from judging one another — why dost thou judge thy brother, seeing we shall all stand there together. Mormon’s use of it is discriminating: all people must surely stand, and the next sentences pronounce woe on those who will not hearken to the words of Jesus and of them whom he hath sent (28:34). The identical clause, with the same universal ‘all’, is turned from a reason not to judge into the warrant of a judgment. The suppressed context is the one that would embarrass the borrowing.

28:31.note: ‘Therefore great and marvellous works shall be wrought by them, before the great and coming day, when all people must surely stand before the judgement seat of Christ.’ Six words from a KJV singleton. The ‘great and marvellous work’ clause of this verse and the next is Isaiah 29:14’s and is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 21:9; the register cross-references it at 28:32.

28:34.text: He that receiveth you receiveth me, and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:40 / John 13:20, with the polarity of Luke 10:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “receiveth him that sent me” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 10:40, Luke 9:48 and John 13:20 — and all three run the chain in the same direction and the same positive form: he that receives the messenger receives me, and he that receives me receives him that sent me. Luke 10:16 is the KJV’s only negative version of the chain, and it uses a different verb: ‘he that despiseth you despiseth me; and he that despiseth me despiseth him that sent me’. 3 Nephi 28:34 has ‘whoso receiveth not the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent, receiveth not him’ — Matthew’s verb in Luke’s polarity. 1830’s relatives ‘them which he hath chosen’ and ‘them which he hath sent’ are modernised to ‘those whom’ in 1920, moving away from the KJV’s ‘which’.
provenance.significance: Two changes and both are pressure on the same point. The KJV’s chain is about receiving persons — ‘he that receiveth you’; 3 Nephi 28:34 makes it about receiving words, twice (‘the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent’). And it adds a terminus none of the four verses has: ‘and therefore he will not receive them at the last day’, which turns the chain around so that the rejected messenger becomes the one who does the rejecting. It is the same move as 3 Nephi 19:23, where believing on the apostles’ words is made the antecedent of believing in Christ rather than its synonym — a claim about the standing of a text and its witnesses, made by rewriting a saying about persons.

28:34.note: ‘And wo be unto him that will not hearken unto the words of Jesus, and also to them which he hath chosen and sent among them: for whoso receiveth not the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent, receiveth not him.’ The Synoptic and Johannine chain of reception, run in the negative and terminated with a clause the KJV does not have.

28:35.text: The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.

provenance.other: “if he had not been born” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:24: ‘it had been good for that man if he had not been born’. The Markan parallel reads ‘good were it for that man if he had never been born’ (Mark 14:21), so the Book of Mormon’s ‘it would be better for them if they had not been born’ is Matthew’s form pluralised, not Mark’s.
provenance.significance: The man of Matthew 26:24 is Judas, and the sentence is passed in the same breath as ‘woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed’. 3 Nephi 28:34 has just pronounced its own woe — on whoever will not hearken to the words of Jesus and of his messengers — and 28:35 completes it with the sentence the KJV reserves for the betrayer. Refusing the record is put on a level with handing Christ over. That reading is strengthened by what the machine turned up two verses into the chapter: the highest-ranked candidate at 28:4 is Matthew 26:15, Judas asking ‘What will ye give me’, which the register declines as coincidence — but it is Matthew 26 that supplies this verse, and the two occurrences frame the chapter.

28:35.note: ‘And it would be better for them if they had not been born.’ Seven words from a KJV singleton, with the singular made plural, applied to those who reject the words of Jesus and of the disciples he has sent.

28:35.text: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?

provenance.route: Hebrews 10:29 for the sense, Matthew 5:13 for the phrase → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sorer punishment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:29, which is also the King James Bible’s only sentence about a person trampling Christ: ‘who hath trodden under foot the Son of God’. “under foot of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:13, of savourless salt. 3 Nephi 28:35 has ‘trampled under feet of men’ — Matthew’s phrase with a plural foot and a different verb; “trample” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Psalm 91:13, Isaiah 63:3, Matthew 7:6) and in none of them is the object a person.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 10:26-29 is the New Testament’s hardest warning about rejecting what one has received — no more sacrifice for sins, a certain looking for of judgment, and a sorer punishment for the man who has trodden under foot the Son of God. That is the argument 3 Nephi 28:34-35 is making: woe to him that will not hearken, and it would be better for him if he had not been born, for the justice of an offended God has been trampled under feet of men. The Book of Mormon says with Matthew’s salt-idiom what Hebrews says of the Son of God, and it substitutes ‘the justice of an offended God’ for Hebrews’ person of the Son.

28:35.note: ‘For do ye suppose that ye can get rid of the justice of an offended God, who hath been trampled under feet of men, that thereby salvation might come?’ The phrase is Matthew 5:13’s (adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 12:13) and the sense is Hebrews 10:29’s; the row records the fusion rather than either half.
28:35.whyNot: No word of Hebrews 10:29 is reproduced — the Book of Mormon has ‘trampled’ where both candidate verses have ‘trodden’, and ‘feet’ where Matthew has ‘foot’. The trampling idiom is common enough in the Book of Mormon that the writer may simply be reusing his own formula, and the connection to Hebrews rests on the shared argument rather than on shared English. Marked uncertain for KJV-specificity for that reason.
